Probably not with unaided eyes.

Although the Moon is geometrically above the horizon, it is an exceptionally thin crescent—only **1.32% illuminated**—and just **13.17° from the Sun**. More importantly, the Sun is still **5.1° above the horizon**, so the sky around the Moon remains very bright. The Moon is also only **16.8° high**, where atmospheric haze and extinction further reduce contrast.

Under exceptionally transparent conditions, an experienced observer might detect such a crescent around or shortly after sunset, but at the stated moment an ordinary observer is **very unlikely** to see it. Your best chance would be roughly **20–35 minutes later**, after the Sun has set but before the Moon gets too low. Use the Sun’s setting point as a guide, but **do not scan near the Sun with binoculars or a telescope while it is above the horizon**.
